title: Foundation for a General Strain Theory of Crime and Delinquency, Criminology 30(1):47-87 (February 1992)
provider: Robert Agnew, American Society of Criminology / Wiley
notes: The founding statement of general strain theory. Full text paywalled. The publisher abstract was retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API, and the Semantic Scholar Graph API returned the abstract together with the article's opening paragraphs. Supports: the three major types of strain as the actual or anticipated failure to achieve positively valued goals, the actual or anticipated removal of positively valued stimuli, and the actual or anticipated presentation of negatively valued stimuli; that the paper distinguishes strain theory from social control and differential association/social learning theory, gives guidelines for measuring strain, and discusses the factors influencing the choice of delinquent versus nondelinquent adaptations; that after dominating deviance research in the 1960s strain theory came under heavy attack in the 1970s, with prominent researchers - Hirschi (1969) and Kornhauser (1978) are the ones Agnew names - suggesting it be abandoned, and that its influence was much diminished by 1992; that most empirical studies then still relied on the models of Merton (1938), A. Cohen (1955), and Cloward and Ohlin (1960); and that Agnew drew on stress research in medical sociology and psychology, equity and justice research in social psychology, and aggression research including recent versions of frustration-aggression. Pagination cross-checked against the NCJRS record (NCJ 136257), which gives 47-87 and a length of 41 pages; Crossref's 47-88 is treated as an exclusive endpoint. No wording reproduced.

title: Building on the Foundation of General Strain Theory: Specifying the Types of Strain Most Likely to Lead to Crime and Delinquency, Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency 38(4):319-361 (November 2001)
provider: Robert Agnew, SAGE Publications
notes: Publisher abstract retrieved verbatim through the Crossref API on 2026-08-19; full text paywalled. Supports two things the lesson needs. First, the four characteristics that make a strain criminogenic: strains are most likely to result in crime when they are seen as unjust, are seen as high in magnitude, are associated with low social control, and create some pressure or incentive to engage in criminal coping. Second, the measurement problem stated by the theory's own author: researchers have little guidance when selecting among the many hundreds of types of strain and have trouble explaining why only some of them are related to crime, and the article predicts that some types of strain that have dominated strain research are not related to crime while some neglected types are. No wording reproduced.

title: Strain, Economic Status, and Crime, chapter 11 in Alex R. Piquero (ed.), The Handbook of Criminological Theory (Wiley, 2015)
provider: Robert Agnew, in John Wiley & Sons
notes: The theory's own author reviewing both classic and general strain theory. Read in full on 2026-08-19; the copy read was a PDF posted on a CUNY BMCC course site (openlab.bmcc.cuny.edu), whose page footer identifies it as Piquero, A. R. (2015), The Handbook of Criminological Theory, John Wiley & Sons, copyright 2015. Supports: that classic strain theory is the tradition of Merton (1938), Cohen (1955) and Cloward and Ohlin (1960) and turns on economic success or the broader goal of middle-class status; that poorer individuals are said to face more goal blockage and relative deprivation; that classic strain theorists held criminal coping more likely among those with weak commitment to legitimate norms, who blame others for their strain, who associate with criminal peers especially gang members, and who have the skills and opportunities for crime; that general strain theory widens strain to any disliked event or condition falling into three groups and distinguishes objective from subjective strains; that strains lead to negative emotions such as anger and frustration which create pressure for corrective action; that criminogenic strains are high in magnitude, touch core goals, values, needs, identities or activities, are seen as unjust, and are easily resolved through crime; the full list of conditioning factors - poor coping skills and resources, few conventional social supports, low social control, disposition to criminal coping including criminal associates, beliefs favourable to crime, and traits such as low constraint and negative emotionality, and situations where the costs of crime seem low and the benefits high; and that studies of economic status and crime have produced mixed results, most suggesting economic status is unrelated or weakly related to individual offending, which prompted challenges to strain theory's validity from Hirschi (1969) and Kornhauser (1978), with Agnew arguing the relationship is modest over much of its range but substantial for the very poor. Copyrighted; no wording reproduced.

title: A New Test of Classic Strain Theory, Justice Quarterly 13(4):681-704 (December 1996)
provider: Robert Agnew, Francis T. Cullen, Velmer S. Burton Jr., T. David Evans and R. Gregory Dunaway, Taylor & Francis
notes: Abstract retrieved through the OpenAlex API on 2026-08-19; publisher site blocked direct retrieval and the full text is paywalled. Supports: that the central variable of classic strain theory is the individual's level of dissatisfaction or frustration with monetary status; that this variable had been ignored in virtually all tests of the theory, which most often measured strain indirectly as the disjunction between aspirations and expectations; that in a sample of adults in Cincinnati dissatisfaction was highest among objectively deprived individuals and those who wanted a lot of money, expected little, and felt relatively deprived; that dissatisfaction had a positive effect on income-generating crime and drug use, strongest among those with criminal friends and beliefs conducive to crime; and that the authors described this as qualified support for classic strain theory unlike the findings in much previous research. No wording reproduced.

Supports Braithwaite's own statement of the distinction in his own words: reintegrative shaming communicates disapproval within a continuum of respect, treating the offender as a good person who did a bad deed, and is forgiving, with ceremonies to decertify deviance terminating ceremonies that certified it; stigmatization is disrespectful shaming that treats the offender as a bad person and leaves the stigma permanently; and his summary claim that forgiving, respectful societies that still take crime seriously have lower crime rates than societies that degrade and humiliate. No wording reproduced.

The Board's own narrative on the same spread states that one estimate of the debris 'was 640 times larger than the data used to calibrate the model' and parenthetically that '(Later analysis showed that the debris object was actually 400 times larger)'; that 'As information gets passed up an organization hierarchy... key explanations and supporting information is filtered out'; and that 'The Board views the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers as an illustration of the problematic methods of technical communication at NASA'. notes: Read to support the origin of the 72 ppi figure: there are 72 points in one inch in both PostScript and CSS; the original Macintosh had a 512x384, roughly 72 ppi display and the OS used that value to map physical measurements to pixels so a typographic point equaled one screen pixel, producing genuine WYSIWYG; the 72 ppi assumption then stuck in software even as later displays reached higher densities (e.g. 91-98 ppi on later Macs), while Windows assumed 96 ppi. Reference-only technical article; no wording reproduced.

title: Moving to Opportunity for Fair Housing Demonstration Program: Final Impacts Evaluation - Executive Summary (November 2011)
provider: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research
notes: PDF downloaded and read in full on 2026-08-19. Supports: MTO's authorization under section 152 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1992 and 1994 launch; enrollment of 4,604 low-income households from 1994 to 1998 in Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York; the three randomized groups and the below-10-percent-poverty restriction on experimental vouchers; the ITT/TOT distinction; baseline tract poverty of about 53 percent and duration-weighted control-group poverty of about 40 percent with ITT reductions of 9 and 7 percentage points; long-term findings of lower extreme obesity, diabetes, psychological distress and major depression among adults; no detectable impacts on work, earnings or other economic outcomes; few statistically significant impacts on educational outcomes or on risky and criminal behavior, with signs of a gender difference among youth and some indication of reduced drug-selling arrests; and the report's own statement that MTO moved families into neighborhoods where neighbors were more willing to work together to support shared norms, a measure of informal social control. Prepared for HUD by outside researchers, so treated as reference-only rather than assumed public domain; nothing reproduced.

title: Moving To Opportunity (program overview and reports index)
provider: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, HUD USER
notes: Read on 2026-08-19. Used to corroborate the design description in the executive summary.

title: Profile (ICC profiles and the profile connection space)
provider: International Color Consortium (color.org)

WebP and AVIF each offer lossy and lossless modes, alpha, and animation; lossy WebP averages 25-35% smaller than comparable JPEG and lossless WebP about 26% smaller than PNG; AVIF generally compresses better than WebP (median ~50% vs ~30%) but has narrower browser support and needs fallbacks via <picture>. Uncompressed scale: a 1920x1080 full-color frame at 4 bytes/pixel = 8,294,400 bytes, ~249 MB per second at 30 fps. H.264/AVC is broadly compatible; H.265/HEVC targets about half the file size of AVC at comparable quality but is less widely supported. Supports: that most modern deterrence theory traces to Beccaria and Bentham and that they identified severity, certainty, and celerity as the three ingredients, with severity alone unable to deter; Beccaria's own view that probability of punishment outweighs cruelty; that only about half of crimes are reported and arrests follow only a small fraction of reported crimes (Blumstein and Beck 1999 offense-to-arrest ratios of roughly four to one for robbery and five to one for burglary); that the incremental deterrent effect of increases in lengthy prison sentences is modest at best; that all evidence on the deterrent effect of certainty pertains to certainty of apprehension rather than post-arrest outcomes, so there is no evidence either way on mandating imprisonment given conviction; that recidivism declines markedly with age and most active career offenders desist typically in their thirties (Farrington 2003), making selective incapacitation hard to implement because high-rate offenders are identifiable retrospectively but not prospectively; and that because incarceration rates themselves depend on crime rates, the committee could not arrive at a precise estimate or even a modest range of estimates of the magnitude of incarceration's effect on crime. notes: Abstract and bibliographic record retrieved in this run from the NCBI E-utilities PubMed record (PMID 11840958); the full text is paywalled and was not read. Cited only for the position the paper takes: the authors, one of whom is Roger Boisjoly himself, examine Edward Tufte's analysis of the event and hold that the Morton Thiokol engineers 'recommended against the launch of Challenger because the projected launch temperature between 26 degrees F to 29 degrees F was far outside their field database of successful launches', that they 'had asked for, but not received, data necessary to determine the cause of massive blow-by on the launch the previous January', and that the engineers 'did what they were ethically as well as professionally obligated to do'. Used to prevent the lesson from overstating any single account of the charts.

title: Psychological debriefing for preventing post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, 2002, Issue 2, CD000560)
provider: Rose S, Bisson J, Churchill R, Wessely S; record and structured abstract via PubMed (PMID 12076399)
notes: Eleven randomized trials of single-session debriefing met inclusion criteria; trial quality was generally poor. No significant short-term (3-5 month) reduction in PTSD risk (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.60-2.46); one trial reported significantly increased PTSD risk at one year (OR 2.88, 95% CI 1.11-7.53); no evidence of reduced general psychological morbidity, depression, or anxiety. Reviewers concluded there is no evidence debriefing prevents PTSD and that compulsory debriefing of trauma victims should cease. This is the anchor for the lesson's Common Mistakes correction. Only the structured abstract was read; the full review is subscription content.

title: Addington v. Texas, 441 U.S. 418 (1979)
provider: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports volume 441 (govinfo)
license: Judicial opinion; edict of government, not subject to copyright
notes: Official U.S. Reports text read in full. The lesson's primary authority for the three-standard continuum: preponderance of the evidence for the typical civil case involving a monetary dispute between private parties, because society has a minimal concern with the outcome and the litigants share the risk of error roughly equally; proof beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal cases, where society imposes almost the entire risk of error upon itself; and an intermediate standard usually combining the words clear, cogent, unequivocal and convincing, typically used in civil cases alleging fraud or other quasi-criminal wrongdoing and in deportation and denaturalization cases. Also used for the holding that a clear and convincing standard is required by the Fourteenth Amendment before indefinite involuntary commitment to a state mental hospital, for the Court's refusal to require beyond a reasonable doubt in that setting, for the observation that states remain free to use a higher standard, and for the Court's candid note that there were no directly relevant empirical studies of how jurors apply the three tests. Burger, C.J., wrote for all participating Members; Powell, J., took no part.

Verified direct phrasing used to ground the lesson: 'Computational thinking builds on the power and limits of computing processes, whether they are executed by a human or by a machine'; 'Computational thinking is a fundamental skill for everyone, not just for computer scientists. To reading, writing, and arithmetic, we should add computational thinking to every child's analytical ability'; 'Computational thinking involves solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior, by drawing on the concepts fundamental to computer science'; 'Computational thinking is using abstraction and decomposition when attacking a large complex task or designing a large complex system'; 'Computational thinking is reformulating a seemingly difficult problem into one we know how to solve'; and the subtitle 'It represents a universally applicable attitude and skill set everyone, not just computer scientists, would be eager to learn and use.' Treated as REFERENCE_ONLY (ACM copyright); only brief attributed quotations used.

title: Program Development by Stepwise Refinement
provider: Niklaus Wirth, Communications of the ACM, Vol. 14, No. 4
license: Copyright ACM
notes: Classic paper (CACM Vol. 14, No. 4, April 1971, pp. 221-227; DOI 10.1145/362575.362577). Bibliographic details confirmed via web search (ACM DL, Semantic Scholar, MIT-hosted copy). Describes top-down program development: state the whole task, decompose it into subtasks, and refine each subtask progressively until it is simple enough to express directly (illustrated with the eight-queens problem). Cited here to ground top-down design / stepwise refinement as the canonical decomposition technique. REFERENCE_ONLY (ACM copyright); facts synthesized in original prose.

title: Blueprint Reading, Chapter 5: Dimensioning Systems (WisTech Open, Wisconsin Technical College System, 2025)
provider: WisTech Open
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Supports the rule that a print must fully define the part so the reader never scales it, that each size appears only once so some distances must be calculated, that dimensions belong on the view showing the profile most clearly and not to hidden lines; and the definitions of datum, datum (baseline) dimensioning, arrowless dimensioning, chain dimensioning, broken-chain dimensioning, and tabular dimensioning, plus decimal-inch, fractional, metric and dual dimensioning and the exact 1 in = 25.4 mm relationship. The chapter's URL slug does not match its chapter number in the book's own navigation.

title: Blueprint Reading, Chapter 9: Print Symbols and Notes (WisTech Open, Wisconsin Technical College System, 2025)
provider: WisTech Open
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Supports general versus local (leader-attached) notes; the feature control frame carrying symbol, tolerance, modifier, and datum references; datum feature symbols identified by letter; basic dimensions as theoretically exact values in a rectangular frame carrying no title-block tolerance; and the grouping of geometric controls into form (straightness, flatness, circularity, cylindricity, with no datum reference), profile of a line and of a surface, orientation (angularity, perpendicularity, parallelism), location (position), and runout (circular and total). Also records that concentricity and symmetry were removed in ASME Y14.5-2018.

title: Blueprint Reading, Chapter 7: Title Blocks (WisTech Open, Wisconsin Technical College System, 2025)
provider: WisTech Open
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Supports the title block's location in the lower right and its contents (title, drawing number, revision, scale, dates, material, drafter), the DRAWING:OBJECT reading of the scale ratio with NTS for not to scale, the general tolerance block applying to unspecified dimensions with more decimal places meaning a tighter tolerance, and revision practice including the revision letter in the title block, the change list on the sheet, revision triangles at the point of change, and the requirement to work from the current revision.

title: Blueprint Reading, Chapter 8: Tolerance on Dimensions (WisTech Open, Wisconsin Technical College System, 2025)
provider: WisTech Open
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Supports: nothing can be produced to an exact theoretical size so tolerance is necessary; equal and unequal bilateral, unilateral, limit, and single-limit MIN/MAX forms; specified versus unspecified (title-block) tolerances; maximum and least material condition for external and internal features; clearance and interference fits; the cost penalty of tolerances tighter than function requires; and the tolerance-accumulation comparison of datum, chain, and broken-chain dimensioning with the plus or minus 0.01 in per-dimension example. All arithmetic used in this lesson was recomputed independently in Bash rather than copied.

title: Blueprint Reading, Chapter 2: Views of an Object (WisTech Open, Wisconsin Technical College System, 2025)
provider: WisTech Open
license: CC BY 4.0
notes: Supports pictorial versus orthographic purpose, view alignment and the 45-degree projection line between top and side views, the glass-box unfolding metaphor, the choice of the most characteristic profile as the front view, the four projection quadrants, the truncated-cone projection symbol used to declare first or third angle (and the alternative of writing the words), third angle as the North American standard since the early 1900s, and the reversal of view positions in first angle. Chapter carries an AI writing tool in its reference list, so every fact used was cross-checked against the LibreTexts CC BY book or the NASA manual.

title: Rethinking Classroom Assessment with Purpose in Mind: Assessment for Learning, Assessment as Learning, Assessment of Learning
provider: Lorna Earl and Steven Katz (Aporia Consulting) with the Western and Northern Canadian Protocol for Collaboration in Education assessment team; Manitoba Education, Citizenship and Youth (2006)
notes: Chapter 2 read in full from the official Manitoba Education PDF. Source for the three purposes of classroom assessment (for, as, of learning) and their definitions, the footnote that some authors use only two categories, the observation that assessment as learning has historically been rare, and the statement that it is very difficult and sometimes impossible to serve three assessment purposes at once. Crown copyright, no open licence stated; facts synthesized, wording original.

title: Compulsory Attendance at School (Charles K. Woltz), Law and Contemporary Problems 20:1, 3-22
provider: Duke University School of Law, Scholarship Repository
notes: Legal-academic survey used for the diffusion of compulsory attendance requirements: Massachusetts first in 1852, about thirty-two states by 1900, Mississippi last in 1918. Bibliographic details confirmed from the repository landing page metadata.

title: The role of tutoring in problem solving
provider: Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G.; Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 17(2), 89-100 (1976)
notes: Primary source for the origin of the scaffolding concept. Bibliographic record verified through the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 932126) and Crossref: title, all three authors, journal, volume 17, issue 2, pages 89-100, DOI as given. The paper itself is behind a publisher paywall; the lesson makes only the attribution claim and the general description of scaffolding as adult support enabling a child to accomplish what is beyond unassisted effort, which is corroborated by the two scaffolding reviews cited alongside it.

title: Demeanor, Crime, and Police Behavior: A Reexamination of the Police Services Study Data, Criminology 34(1):83-105 (1996)
provider: Robert E. Worden and Robin L. Shepard; Criminology (American Society of Criminology / Wiley)
notes: Bibliographic record and the publisher-deposited abstract retrieved through the Crossref API; the full text is paywalled and was not read. Cited only for what the abstract states: that recent research had questioned the conclusion that arrest becomes more likely when suspects display a disrespectful or hostile demeanor, and that the authors' reanalysis of the Police Services Study data found the original findings held insofar as the data permitted them to address the criticisms. No claim is made in the lesson about effect sizes or model specifications.

title: Equivalency of the diagnostic accuracy of the PHQ-8 and PHQ-9: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis
provider: Wu Y, Levis B, Riehm KE, et al.; Psychological Medicine 2020;50(8):1368-1380 (author manuscript on PMC)
notes: Full text read on PMC. Supports the point that an individual item on a symptom scale is not a risk assessment: the PHQ-9 item asks about thoughts of being better off dead or of hurting oneself and does not query suicidality specifically; across four studies in non-psychiatric settings (veterans in primary care, coronary artery disease patients, cancer patients), 7% to 21% of participants endorsed the item, but of those only 18% to 35% reported thoughts of suicide on questions designed specifically to assess suicide risk and only 3% to 20% reported a plan. Author manuscript deposited in PMC with no open licence; only reported figures cited.

title: Assisting Students Struggling with Mathematics: Intervention in the Elementary Grades (WWC Practice Guide, March 2021)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Federal practice guide read from the WWC practice guide page. Used for the first recommendation - provide systematic instruction during intervention to develop student understanding of mathematical ideas - and its strong evidence rating, as the clearest current U.S. federal endorsement of structured, guided instruction for students who are struggling. The lesson states explicitly that the guide rates practices for a specific population, not philosophies of learning. Reproduction terms were not separately verified, so it is recorded reference only.

title: Encouraging Girls in Math and Science (IES Practice Guide, NCER 2007-2003)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education (panel chaired by Diane F. Halpern)
notes: Recommendation list and evidence levels read from the IES practice-guide page and cross-checked against the full text of ERIC ED498581. Released September 2007. Supports the recommendation to teach that academic abilities are expandable and improvable (moderate evidence) and the recommendation to provide prescriptive, informational feedback (moderate evidence). Used in the lesson as a dated federal recommendation predating the large-scale mindset trials, not as current support for mindset interventions.

title: Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School (IES Practice Guide, NCEE 2014-4012, April 2014)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Practice guide page read for the four recommendations and their assigned levels of evidence: teach a set of academic vocabulary words intensively across several days using a variety of instructional activities (strong); integrate oral and written English language instruction into content-area teaching (strong); provide regular structured opportunities to develop written language skills (minimal); provide small-group instructional intervention to students struggling in literacy and English language development (moderate). Used so the lesson's advice on multilingual learners rests on rated federal evidence rather than assertion. Reproduction terms not separately verified, so recorded reference only.

title: Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning (IES Practice Guide, September 2007, NCER 2007-2004)
provider: Pashler, H. (chair), Bain, P., Bottge, B., Graesser, A., Koedinger, K., McDaniel, M., Metcalfe, J.; National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Federal practice guide used for the recommendation-level evidence ratings, verified against the full guide text (Table 2 and the per-recommendation 'Level of evidence' statements): spacing moderate; interleaving worked examples with problem solving moderate; combining graphics with verbal descriptions moderate; connecting abstract and concrete representations moderate; 5a pre-questions low; 5b quizzes to re-expose students to key content strong (nine K-12 experiments, more than 30 college experiments, plus a large laboratory literature); 6a delayed judgments of learning low; 6b using tests to identify content needing study low; 7 deep explanatory questions strong. No wording reproduced. Also used for Recommendation 2 (interleaving worked example solutions with problem-solving exercises, moderate evidence) as the classroom form of learning from a symbolic model.

title: WWC Review of the Report 'Effects of Problem Based Economics on High School Economics Instruction' (June 2012)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education; ERIC ED533124
notes: Full PDF retrieved from the ERIC full-text service and read directly. Reviews the randomized trial reported in NCEE 2010-4002 (128 teachers from 106 schools in Arizona and California; analytic sample of 64 teachers after high teacher attrition). Used for: the rating that the study meets WWC evidence standards with reservations; the finding of no statistically significant difference in grade 11-12 students' economics knowledge; and the effect size of 0.29, which the WWC describes as positive and large enough to be considered substantively important under its threshold of at least 0.25 standard deviations.

title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom (WWC Practice Guide, September 2008)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Federal practice guide used for the claim that antecedent-behavior-consequence analysis and teaching plus reinforcing replacement behaviors appear in official U.S. guidance, and for the recommendation evidence levels (modifying the classroom environment and teaching/reinforcing new skills rated strong; identifying triggers, collaborating with colleagues and families, and schoolwide strategies rated moderate). Reuse terms for the document were not separately verified, so it is recorded as reference only.

title: Assisting Students Struggling with Reading: Response to Intervention (RtI) and Multi-Tier Intervention in the Primary Grades (IES Practice Guide, NCEE 2009-4045, February 2009)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Full guide text read from the IES-hosted PDF (rti_reading_pg_021809.pdf) and cross-checked against the WWC practice guide page. Used for Recommendation 1 (screen all students at the beginning and middle of the year; rated moderate evidence) and Recommendation 2 (provide differentiated reading instruction for all students based on assessments of students' current reading levels, tier 1), whose level of evidence the panel judged low and which rests on descriptive-correlational work in which reading growth was higher for teachers who implemented the differentiation program with greater fidelity. Reproduction terms not separately verified, so recorded reference only.

title: Using Student Achievement Data to Support Instructional Decision Making (IES Practice Guide, NCEE 2009-4067, September 2009)
provider: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education
notes: Practice guide summary read from the WWC practice guide page. Used for the five recommendations, chiefly 'make data part of an ongoing cycle of instructional improvement', and for the fact that every recommendation in the guide carries the lowest evidence rating the WWC assigns. Cited to show that federal panels recommend assessment-driven instructional adjustment while rating the evidence for it as weak. Verified additionally from the published PDF: a Low rating means no body of research demonstrating effects on achievement was identified, and is not a judgment that the recommendation is unimportant.

title: Rate Fences: Definition / Meaning
provider: Xotels (glossary)
notes: Industry glossary read via WebFetch. Corroborates that rate fences are conditions attached to a rate (advance-booking cutoffs, non-refundable payment, minimum/maximum length of stay, channel and product restrictions) used to protect standard rates. Commercial source; REFERENCE_ONLY, no wording reproduced.

title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
provider: Yeager, D. S., et al., Nature 573, 364-369, 2019
notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API and the open PMC full text read directly (PMC6786290). Source of the 12,490 students / 65 schools design, the 0.10 grade-point core-GPA gain for lower-achieving students (95% CI 0.04-0.16), the rise in advanced tenth-grade mathematics enrolment from 33% to 36%, the peer-norm moderation, and the preregistration and blinded Bayesian corroboration.

title: Academic Self-Efficacy and Academic Performance in Online Learning: A Mini Review (Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 2794)
provider: Satoru Yokoyama; Frontiers Media
license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the article page)
notes: Peer-reviewed mini review used for the summary of the meta-analytic literature: academic self-efficacy is positively associated with academic performance across a large body of studies (Honicke and Broadbent's 53-study review found only six with no significant correlation), and longitudinal meta-analysis indicates the relationship runs in both directions over time. Used to support the lesson's caution that the correlation does not by itself license a one-way causal claim.

title: Exploring the Boundaries of the Criminal Courtroom Workgroup
provider: Common Law World Review (Richard Young), volume 42, issue 3, pages 203-239
notes: Full text is paywalled; only the publisher-supplied abstract retrieved through the Crossref API was read. Supports the narrow claim that the courtroom workgroup has become a standard way of explaining decision patterns and dynamics in criminal trial courts in common law jurisdictions, and that the framework centres on interdependent relationships among workgroup members. Not used for any empirical claim about U.S. courts.

title: What explains community coalition effectiveness? A review of the literature
provider: Zakocs RC, Edwards EM; American Journal of Preventive Medicine 30(4):351-361
notes: Published abstract read through the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 16530624); full text is paywalled. Supports the review scope (1980-2004, 26 qualifying studies from 1168 citations screened), the counts of effectiveness indicators (26 indicators, 19 measuring coalition functioning, 2 measuring community-wide health behaviour change), the six coalition-building factors associated with effectiveness in five or more studies, and the authors' own caution about inconsistent measurement and cross-sectional designs. No wording reused.

title: Social Work and the Environment: Understanding People and Place
provider: Michael Kim Zapf, Critical Social Work 11(3) (2010)
license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
notes: Peer-reviewed open-access critique (journal states CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; no-derivatives, so treated as reference only). Full text read. Supports: person-in-environment is described as the profession's conventional metaphor/perspective rather than a predictive theory, and the 'environment' in mainstream social work usage repeatedly collapses into the social environment with the physical and built environment dropping out unremarked. Used for the precision points about what PIE is and what its standard reading leaves out.

title: Problems and Strategies in Services Marketing
provider: Journal of Marketing (Zeithaml, Parasuraman & Berry)
notes: Zeithaml, V.A., Parasuraman, A. & Berry, L.L. (1985), Journal of Marketing 49(2):33-46. Classic statement of the IHIP characteristics (intangibility, heterogeneity, inseparability, perishability). Verified from bibliographic records; copyrighted, not reproduced.
